content: Scabies is a highly contagious skin condition caused by a microscopic mite. It is characterized by intense itching, particularly at night, and the presence of rashes, often located between the fingers. Scratching and digging at the skin can lead to sores or abrasions. Thin, pencil-like burrow lines may also appear on the skin. In infants, the mites can spread more extensively, causing pimples on the trunk or small blisters on the palms and soles. In young children, the head, neck, shoulders, palms, and soles are commonly affected, while in older children and adults, the hands, wrists, genitals, and abdomen are more frequently involved. Scabies is transmitted through direct skin-to-skin contact with an infected individual and, less commonly, through shared clothing or bedding. Entire families can sometimes be affected. Outbreaks are more prevalent in settings such as nursing homes, long-term care facilities, and childcare centers. The mites burrow into the skin, laying eggs that mature within 21 days. The itching and rash associated with scabies are due to an allergic reaction to the mites. Individuals at highest risk for scabies include those who have close physical contact with an infected person. Pets and animals do not transmit human scabies. It is also unlikely for scabies to spread through swimming pools or contact with towels, bedding, or clothing unless the infected person has a severe form known as crusted scabies. You should seek medical attention if you experience symptoms of scabies or if someone you have been in close contact with has been diagnosed with the condition. Diagnosis typically involves a physical examination of the skin, and in some cases, skin scrapings from a burrow are examined under a microscope to identify the mites. A skin biopsy may also be performed. Treatment for scabies usually involves prescription medicated creams, with permethrin 5% being the most commonly used. Other options include benzyl benzoate, sulfur in petrolatum, and crotamiton. Lindane is rarely used due to its potential side effects. These creams are applied to the entire body, and treatment may need to be repeated after one week. It is essential to treat all household members or sexual partners of the infected person, even if they do not show symptoms. Personal items such as underwear, towels, and sleepwear should be washed in hot water, and carpets and upholstered furniture should be vacuumed. For more severe cases, oral medications like ivermectin may be prescribed. Itching may persist for up to two weeks or longer after treatment begins but will resolve if the treatment plan is followed. Cool soaks, calamine lotion, and oral antihistamines can help alleviate itching. Most cases of scabies can be successfully treated without long-term complications. However, severe cases with extensive scaling or crusting may indicate an underlying condition such as HIV. Intense scratching can lead to secondary skin infections, such as impetigo. To prevent scabies, avoid direct contact with infected individuals.
